title: Impulse Anvil
text: Impulse Anvil DESIGN THE IR ITSELF Impulse Anvil lets you take IRs, recordings and found sounds , reshape them, combine them, and save the result as a new WAV impulse response. Load → Shape → Combine → Edit → Bake → Reuse Where do you want to start? Make something in 5 minutes Load a sound, change it, and Bake your first IR. Try creative recipes Phase tricks, found sounds, recursive Bakes and multi morph stereo worlds. Combine A and B Choose how two sources become one new response. Draw movement & route time Draw your own A→B transition or use Path to move forward and backward through source time. The basic idea A normal convolution workflow often starts with: Which IR do I want to use? Impulse Anvil adds another step: What IR do I want to make? A room IR can be your starting point. So can a guitar cabinet, a metal hit, a voice, a scrape, a field recording, or another IR you already created in Anvil. Once you hear something worth keeping, press Bake . The result becomes a WAV IR you can use again. How these docs are written The main pages use producer language: what a control does, what changes in the sound, and what to try. Deeper DSP details stay inside Technical background sections so the normal workflow remains quick to read.

title: 5-Minute Quickstart
text: 5 Minute Quickstart Make one IR, hear what it does, and the rest of the plugin becomes easier to place. 1. Put Anvil on a track Use a sound you know well: guitar, piano, synth, drums or voice. A fairly dry source makes the effect easiest to judge. Keep the listening level sensible while experimenting. Unusual IRs can create strong resonances. 2. Load something into A Click Load in A, or drag a compatible audio file onto the A panel. Try a factory IR, one of your own IRs, or a recording. Click the A panel to hear A. !!! tip "Want a fast starting point?" Press the small Random button beside A's Load control. It can choose another available IR and give the slot a new treatment without randomly boosting Gain. 3. Change one thing Start with: Time — shorter or longer Color — add a changed copy back into the IR Texture — let that Color idea build into more layers Move one control and listen to what changes. 4. Add B Load something different into B. Click the Morph panel and move Morph. Start with Time Morph , then compare another Morph mode. 5. Add movement Enable A→B Lerp . Use: Lerp Start to choose when the movement begins Lerp Time to choose how long the movement takes Both are shown in milliseconds. For a custom transition, choose Draw and paint the A→B movement directly. 6. Keep only the useful part In EDIT , move Start and End around the part you want. Start before End = forward Start after End = reverse link them = scan one fixed size window through the IR Need tiny movements? Shift + drag = fine Ctrl + drag = very fine 7. Bake it When you hear something worth keeping, press Bake . The exported WAV can be used in another compatible convolution plugin, loaded back into Anvil, or combined with another result. !!! example "Good first experiment" Record a short metal hit, clap, scrape or object impact. Find an interesting region in EDIT, Bake it, then load that Bake back into Anvil and Morph it with a completely different IR.

title: Interface Basics
text: Interface Basics A few interaction rules make the whole plugin faster to use. Click the panel you want to hear A, B and Morph are also your listening navigation. click A to hear A click B to hear B click Morph to hear the combined result The active panel is highlighted. A and B each have Normalize Normalize A and Normalize B work separately. Use them when one source arrives much quieter or louder than the other. Gain still works with Normalize enabled , so you can normalize first and then deliberately make A or B stronger. Fine movement Shift + drag = fine Ctrl + drag = very fine This is especially useful for millisecond controls such as Start/End, Lerp timing and Color Offset. Hold the key before you start dragging. Hover for quick help The main controls now include short tooltips. Hover Time, Color, Morph, Lerp, EDIT, EQ, OUT or the playback controls for a quick explanation of what that control changes. Random means "try another idea here" Each Random button only changes the area it belongs to. A / B Random beside Load Can choose another available IR and change that slot's Time, Color and Texture. Gain returns to 0 dB instead of being randomly boosted. Normalize stays as you set it. A / B Random beside Color Keeps the current file and tries a new Time/Color/Texture treatment. Morph Random Tries another A/B relationship. EQ Random Changes EQ only. EDIT Random Tries another slice/edit setup. OUT Random Creates a broader finishing variation across EDIT, EQ and Width while protecting the main playback level controls. IR Library and manual Load The IR Library can collect several locations in one menu: bundled Factory IRs Factory/User folders from older setups Baked IRs Expansions a Custom IR Folder When you use Load WAV… , Anvil remembers the folder you browsed and starts there next time. Use Choose Custom IR Folder… when you keep a personal IR library somewhere else. Double click a title to reset that section Color → reset Color/Texture EQ → reset EQ EDIT → reset EDIT OUT → reset OUT utilities Reset everything except the loaded files Use: Options → Init / Reset Controls (keep IRs) Your A and B files stay loaded.

title: Appearance & Themes
text: Appearance & Themes Impulse Anvil includes built in themes and a theme editor. Open: Options → Design Choose a built in theme Pick any built in design from the Design menu. The theme changes the interface only. It does not change the audio. Customize the current theme Choose: Options → Design → Customize Current Theme… The editor has two layers. Global colors Global colors create the base look for the whole plugin. Panel specific colors A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT can each override the Global colors. Choose a panel and enable Use panel specific colours . That panel can then have its own: panel color border color accent highlight knob color text color Leave the override off when you want that panel to inherit the Global theme. Create a theme from an image with AI A Theme Schema 2 file can also act as a template for AI assisted design. Export the current theme, give that JSON to an AI together with an image whose mood or palette you like, and ask it to generate a compatible Impulse Anvil theme from the reference. Then paste the returned JSON into the exported file and import it back into Anvil. Save and reuse a theme The Design menu can: use saved user themes import Theme JSON export the current theme set the current theme as default reset to Anvil Blue Export creates a complete JSON theme that can be edited or shared and then imported again. After a successful export, Show File opens the exported file in Explorer. !!! tip "Using AI to recolor a theme" Export the current theme first. Give that JSON to the AI and ask it to change only the color values while keeping the structure and required keys intact. Import the returned JSON into Anvil and inspect the result. ??? info "Technical background" Current exports use Theme Schema 2. A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT each have an enabled flag plus panel, panelStroke, accent, highlight, knob and text colors. Disabled panel blocks inherit the Global theme. Older compatible themes remain supported.

title: Install & Activate
text: Install & Activate Windows VST3 installation 1. Close your DAW. 2. Extract the Impulse Anvil ZIP. 3. Copy the complete Impulse Anvil.vst3 folder to C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3\ . 4. Open your DAW and rescan VST3 plug ins if required. Activate the full license 1. Open Impulse Anvil. 2. Click Demo / Activate . 3. Paste the license key supplied with your purchase. 4. Click Activate . Activation requires an internet connection. After a signed entitlement has been issued, the plugin supports offline use with periodic background validation. Important project note If a DAW project uses WAV files loaded from external locations, keep those files available at the same paths. A preset/session stores their paths; moving or deleting the source files can prevent exact restoration.

title: What Impulse Anvil Does
text: What Impulse Anvil Does Impulse Anvil is for making impulse responses , not only loading them. A normal convolution workflow is often: pick an IR → put sound through it Anvil adds the creative part before that: load IRs or recordings → change them → combine them → listen → Bake a new IR You can start with almost anything useful Try: a room or cabinet IR; another IR you already designed; a metal hit; a voice or breath; a scrape; a field recording; a short noise or texture; a tiny section taken from a much longer recording. The source does not need to sound like a reverb before you load it. What Anvil lets you do A and B hold two independent starting materials. Time makes them shorter or longer. Color adds changed copies back into the IR. Texture repeats that Color idea in deeper layers. Morph decides how A and B become one new response. A→B Lerp lets the IR itself move from A toward B over time. EDIT searches, cuts, reverses and fades the part you actually want. EQ and Width shape the final IR. Bake saves what you made as a reusable WAV. Why Bake matters Bake turns an experiment into new raw material. You can make: then load C back in: and continue. That is why Impulse Anvil can create results that no single original IR contained. ??? info "Technical background" Convolution can use any compatible audio waveform as its impulse response data. Short material often behaves more like a complex tonal/filter fingerprint; longer material can add stronger time, resonance and decay behavior. Anvil uses that freedom deliberately for sound design instead of limiting the source material to measured acoustic spaces.

title: What Gets Baked?
text: What Gets Baked? There is one rule worth learning: Some controls change the IR you are making. Other controls only change how you hear the plugin. These become part of the IR A/B → Time → Color / Texture → Slot Normalize → Slot Gain → Morph / Lerp → EDIT → IR In → EQ → Width → Normalize → Limiter → Bake If you change something in that chain, you are changing the response that can be saved. These are only for playback The following controls do not become part of the baked WAV: Input Wet Level Dry / Wet Out They only change how Anvil sounds on the track while you are working. !!! tip "Simple example" If the WAV you Bake is too quiet, change IR In or the IR's Normalize/Gain path. Turning up Out only makes the plugin louder while you listen; it does not make the exported IR louder. ??? info "Technical background" Anvil prepares and caches the processed impulse response before final track playback. Dry/wet mixing and final output gain happen afterwards, so they cannot change the exported IR data.

title: IR A / IR B
text: IR A / IR B A and B are two independent source lanes. They can hold measured IRs, designed IRs or compatible recordings. Choose what you are listening to The current interface uses the panels themselves as navigation: click A to hear A; click B to hear B; click Morph to hear A and B through the current Morph setup. There is no separate user facing "A Only" / "B Only" workflow to learn. Load a source Use Load or drag a WAV/AIFF/FLAC file directly onto the A or B panel. The whole card accepts drops. Use the previous/next arrows to step through discovered IR files. Time A / Time B Changes the duration of that source before Color, Texture and Morph. Below 1.0 = shorter/faster. 1.0 = original duration. Above 1.0 = longer/slower. Normalize A / Normalize B A and B have independent Normalize switches . Turn Normalize on when one source is much quieter or louder than the other and you want a more even starting point before Morph. Gain Gain still works even with Normalize enabled . Normalize creates the reference level first; Gain lets you intentionally make A or B more dominant afterwards. Random discovery Random beside Load Chooses another available IR and randomizes the slot's Time, Color and Texture . It does not randomly boost Gain: Gain returns to 0 dB . Your Normalize switch stays as you set it. Random beside Color Keeps the current file but randomizes its Time, Color and Texture settings. Use it when you like the source itself but want a new treatment. Reset the slot's creative layer Double click the Color header in A or B to reset that slot's Color and Texture controls without replacing the loaded source. ??? info "Technical background" The slot processing order is Time → Color/Texture → per slot Normalize → Gain. During two slot processing, sample rate differences are resolved as required before A/B construction.

title: Color & Texture
text: Color & Texture Color and Texture are where one IR can start turning into something it was not before. Color Color makes a changed copy of the current IR and mixes that copy back in. That gives you three simple questions: Time — how different should the copy's timing be? Leave Time near 1.00 for small differences. Move it further away when you want the copy to become obviously shorter or longer. Very small differences around 1.00 can create phasey, metallic or comb like tone changes because the original IR and its altered copy interfere with each other. Offset — how much later should the copy begin? Small Offset values can make the interference change dramatically. Larger values can feel more like a separate ghost event, reflection or slap inside the IR. Offset ranges from 0–500 ms. The first few milliseconds are useful for phase/comb color; the wider range can create clearly separated reflections and rhythmic spacing. Amount — how much of the copy do you want? Start lower than you think. The useful point is often where you notice the new character without losing the original IR completely. C1 and C2 A and B each have two Color layers. That means you can create one subtle extra layer with C1 and then use C2 for something different—for example: C1 very close in Time for a phasey tone; C2 further away with Offset for a second reflection or texture. Texture Depth Texture repeats the Color idea in generations. Think: Color makes another version. Texture lets that version make another version. 0 = off 1 = one extra generation 2–4 = deeper and denser Start at 1. More depth is not automatically better. !!! example "Try this: instant phase color" 1. Load any IR into A. 2. Enable C1 . 3. Leave Offset at 0. 4. Move C1 Time only slightly away from 1.00 — for example 0.95 or 1.05. 5. Slowly adjust Amount. Tiny Time differences can completely change the tone. The exact useful value depends on the IR. Random and reset The small Random button beside Color keeps the current file and tries a new Time/Color/Texture treatment. Double click Color to reset Color and Texture for that slot without replacing the loaded IR. ??? info "Technical background" A Color layer is a time resampled, delayed and gain scaled copy of the slot that is summed back with the original. When two closely related versions are combined, their timing differences create frequency dependent reinforcement and cancellation—what you hear as phasey or comb like coloration. Texture recursively feeds each new Color generation into the next.

title: Morph & A→B Lerp
text: Morph & A→B Lerp Morph is where A and B become one new impulse response . The Morph control sets the A/B balance. The selected Morph mode decides how the two sources are combined. The six Morph modes Time Morph The most direct blend. A and B meet through their actual time domain shapes. Useful for: clear transitions, natural crossfades and an easy reference point before trying the other modes. Spectral Combines more of the tonal/frequency fingerprint of A and B. Useful for: fused tones where the result feels less like two IRs simply mixed together. Spectral BandSwap Different frequency areas can lean toward different sources. Useful for: hybrids where one part of the spectrum carries more A while another carries more B. Spectral ZigZag Creates a more divided, artificial spectral relationship. Useful for: sharper synthetic colors, unstable tones and more obviously transformed material. Stereo Slot Swap The left and right sides travel through A and B in opposite directions. Useful for: asymmetrical stereo fields and wide A/B relationships. Mid/Side Boundary A forms more of the center foundation while B enters the side field. Useful for: keeping a strong middle while building a different texture around it. Morph Random The small Random button in Morph tries another A/B relationship without replacing the A or B files. It can change the Morph position, Morph mode, Curve/K, Align and Lerp state. Align Align moves the dominant peaks of A and B toward a shared start before they are combined. This can make attacks meet more cleanly. Align can also remove material that existed before the moved peak. If an IR has a useful lead in, swell, scrape or early texture before its main hit, compare Align on and off. Align on: tighter meeting point Align off: keep the original start timing and lead in A→B Lerp Normal Morph gives you one fixed A/B position. A→B Lerp builds movement inside the IR itself : The selected Morph mode is used during that movement. Lerp Start Sets the exact time where the transition begins. 0 ms starts at the beginning of the IR. Lerp Time Sets how long the transition takes. 0 ms creates an instant switch at Lerp Start. The available Start/Time range follows the current prepared A/B length. If Time, Color or Texture makes the endpoints longer, the Lerp timing range follows that growth. Use the A and B waveforms as a map The curve display shows the A and B waveforms behind the transition area. This makes Draw and Path easier to place by eye. You can recognize: a strong transient; a quiet gap; a dense section; a tail; a later reflection or event; and draw the transition or Path around those visible landmarks. If A and B have different lengths, the waveforms also make it obvious where one source has already ended. Curve shapes Choose Linear, Exp, Log, S Curve, Draw or Path . The built in curves shape the A→B movement automatically. Draw lets you paint that movement yourself. Path also lets you control which point in source time is read, including moving backward through earlier material. Bake A→B Lerp uses the same visible Bake button as the rest of Anvil. Preview the result, then Bake when you want to keep it. ??? info "Technical background" The longer prepared A/B endpoint defines the main Lerp source domain. Absolute Lerp Start and Time are clamped to the current available endpoint duration. Time Morph can run as a continuous time varying blend; the spectral/spatial modes use mode aware rendering so Preview and Bake share the same prepared result.

title: Curves, Draw & Path
text: Curves, Draw & Path The Curve area controls how A→B movement develops over time . For Draw and Path, the graph reads: Vertical position = A/B blend. Time normally moves from left to right. Built in curves Linear Moves from A toward B at a steady rate. Exp Spends more of the transition closer to one end, then changes faster later. Use K to strengthen or soften the curve. Log Moves more strongly earlier, then settles toward the other end. Use K to adjust the shape. S Curve Creates a smoother slow fast slow transition. Draw Lets you paint the A/B movement directly. Path Lets you paint both A/B movement and source time travel . Draw Choose Draw in the Curve menu. Drag across the graph to paint the transition. bottom = A top = B left to right = the Lerp timeline The Draw curve is saved with plugin state, presets and DAW sessions. Switching to another curve does not erase your Draw shape. Draw tools The small buttons under the graph are: U — Undo the last edit S — Smooth the shape N — show precision nodes F — Free endpoints R — Reset to a straight A→B line N — precision nodes Enable N when you want exact control. drag a node to reshape the curve double click empty curve space to add a node double click an internal node to remove it Shift + drag = fine Ctrl + drag = very fine F — Free endpoints With F off, Draw begins on A and finishes on B. With F on , the first and last blend can sit anywhere between A and B. Example: Outside the active Lerp timing window, Free Draw holds the authored start/end blend instead of forcing pure A or B. Turning F off restores the endpoints to A and B while keeping the interior Draw shape. Path Path changes the meaning of the horizontal direction. In Path mode: x / left right = which point in source time is being read y / bottom top = A/B blend the order you draw = playback order in the new IR Forward motion Move right: Anvil reads later source time normally. Backward motion Move left during the Path: The new IR goes back and reads earlier source time again. That creates reversed/replayed sections inside the rendered response. Why Path can make the IR longer A straight Path from left to right uses the normal Lerp duration. Backtracking adds travel: That extra horizontal travel becomes extra output time. The length increase comes from the route itself, not from an automatic stretch. Path tools The same tools remain available: U — Undo S — smooth the A/B vertical movement while keeping the forward/backward time route N — precision Path nodes F — free the A/B blend at the beginning/end R — restore a straight forward A→B Path In N mode, internal Path nodes can cross left or right past neighboring x positions. Their order stays intact, so backward time sections remain part of the route. Lerp Start and Lerp Time Path operates inside the current Lerp window. Lerp Start chooses where that window begins. Lerp Time chooses the normal forward span available to the Path. If the Path backtracks, the final rendered IR can become longer than Lerp Time because it travels through part of that source time more than once. Use the waveforms as visual landmarks The graph shows the A and B waveforms behind the Draw/Path area. That means the drawing surface is also a visual map of the source material. For example, you can see a transient or tail in A and deliberately draw the Path so it: reaches B around that event; returns to an earlier visible section; stays near A through one region; crosses toward B around another recognizable shape. This is especially useful in Path mode because you can line up forward/backward time movement with actual visible events in the IR instead of drawing blindly. Preview and Bake Path Preview and Bake use the same rendered Path result. Bake exports what the prepared IR is currently doing, including the authored forward/backward route. ??? info "Technical background" Path stores an ordered 2 D route. Horizontal travel is accumulated by absolute x distance, so leftward travel is preserved rather than sorted away. Each output position maps to source time x and A/B blend y. A straight 0→1 route is duration neutral; horizontal backtracking adds mapped frames. Output remains bounded by Anvil's prepared IR safety limits.

title: Edit
text: Edit EDIT is your IR scanner and cutter . It lets you search through a long prepared IR or recording, keep only the interesting part, reverse it if you want, and Bake that fragment as a new IR. Start and End Normal slice When Start is before End , Anvil keeps that region and plays it forward. Reverse slice When Start is after End , Anvil keeps the region between them and plays it backwards. Scan one fixed size window through a recording The small link control between Start and End locks the current window length. 1. Choose a useful size—perhaps 20 ms, 100 ms or 500 ms. 2. Enable the link. 3. Move Start or End. 4. The other endpoint follows automatically. 5. Listen while the window travels through the recording. 6. Stop when you find a useful spot. 7. Bake it if you want that fragment as its own reusable WAV IR. A single long recording can contain many completely different short convolution fingerprints. Fine millisecond movement Shift + drag = fine movement. Ctrl + drag = very fine movement. Hold the modifier before starting the drag. EDIT Random The small Random button in EDIT tries another edit setup automatically. It can choose short or long regions, move the slice, change fades/predelay and sometimes reverse the region. Fade In / Fade Out Use fades when a cut begins or ends too abruptly. 0 ms means exactly 0 ms. That endpoint stays unshaped. This is especially useful for very short IRs, hard transients and exact cuts. Fade Out + The + option flips the fade out behavior into a swell/stutter style ending rather than the normal fade toward silence. Pre Adds time before the edited IR begins. Reset EDIT Double click the EDIT title to return the editing section to its normal defaults. ??? info "Technical background" Start/End are absolute endpoints on the prepared IR. The selected range is resolved first, fades are applied to that slice, and predelay is inserted afterwards. In 1.0.121 no hidden authored head/tail micro fade is added when the user fade value is 0 ms.
snippet: Edit EDIT is your IR scanner and cutter . It lets you search through a long prepared IR or recording, keep only the interesting part, reverse it if you want, and Bake tha…

title: EQ & Output
text: EQ & Output This section has two jobs: 1. finish the IR you are building 2. control how the plugin plays on your track The difference matters when you Bake. These change the IR IR In Changes the level going into the final IR shaping stage. Use this when the actual response you want to Bake is too quiet or too strong. HP / LP Remove unwanted lows or highs from the IR. Tilt A broad darker/brighter control. Bell 1 / 2 / 3 Use the three bell filters when one frequency area needs a more focused change. Width 0.0 = much narrower / toward mono 1.0 = keep the current width 2.0 = wider Width becomes part of the baked IR. Normalize Brings the final IR up to a consistent peak level. Limiter Adds a safety ceiling to the prepared IR. These only change playback Input Changes the dry/input side of what you hear. Wet Level Changes how loud the convolved result plays. Dry / Wet Changes the balance between the original track and convolution. Out Changes the final plugin output level. None of these four become part of the baked WAV. !!! tip "Baked IR too quiet?" Change IR In , IR Gain/Normalize, or the actual IR processing. Do not turn up Out expecting the WAV to change. Random and reset EQ Random changes only the EQ. OUT Random tries a broader finishing variation across EDIT, EQ and Width while protecting the main playback level controls. Double click EQ to reset EQ. Double click OUT to reset the OUT/utility section. ??? info "Technical background" EQ, Width, final IR Normalize and limiting are applied to the prepared response before it reaches the convolver/export stage. Input, Wet Level, Dry/Wet and final Out are applied later in the track playback path.
snippet: EQ & Output This section has two jobs: 1. finish the IR you are building 2. control how the plugin plays on your track The difference matters when you Bake. These change …

title: Bake & Export
text: Bake & Export Bake means: Keep this IR. Whatever prepared response you are hearing can be turned into a reusable WAV. What Bake keeps Bake can include: A or B preparation Time Color and Texture per slot Normalize and Gain Morph A→B Lerp Draw or Path movement Start/End slicing or reverse slicing fades and Pre IR In EQ Width final IR Normalize IR side Limiter What Bake does not keep These controls only affect how the plugin plays on your track: Input Wet Level Dry / Wet Out Export format Impulse Anvil writes the result as a 32 bit floating point WAV . After export The completion window shows where the file was saved. Press Show File to reveal it directly in Explorer. Use the result anywhere A baked IR can be: loaded back into A or B combined with another Anvil Bake used in another compatible convolution plugin used in an IR loader that accepts standard WAV impulse responses This is where recursive design starts: Baking Lerp, Draw and Path There is one visible Bake button. If A→B Lerp, Draw or Path is active in the prepared result, Bake includes it. Path's forward/backward source time route is rendered into the exported IR as part of the prepared response. ??? info "Technical background" Bake writes the current prepared IR as 32 bit float WAV. The prepared IR chain is bounded by a 30 second safety budget at ordinary sample rates. Final track playback mixing happens afterwards and is not embedded in the WAV.

title: Creative Workflows
text: Creative Workflows This is the tips, tricks and experiments section. The normal manual explains what every part of Anvil does. Creative Workflows answers a different question: What can I actually make with it? These are recipes, not rules. Start with the values shown, then move them by ear. Create a theme from an image with AI Export Theme Schema 2, use any visual reference for mood and color, then import the generated design. Draw your own A→B movement Paint a custom transition, return toward A, and free the start/end blend. Bend time with Path Move forward, travel back through earlier source time, then continue forward again. Phase & comb textures with Color Tiny Time and Offset differences can turn almost any IR into a new tonal filter. Turn recordings into IR material Search through metal, voice, room and field recordings for useful fragments. Recursive Baking Bake a result, load it back in, then build another generation. Multi Morph Stereo Worlds Stack different spatial Morph ideas across generations for complex stereo fields. The recipe format Every workflow follows the same structure: Goal — what you are trying to hear Build it — the shortest useful setup Listen for — what matters more than the numbers Push it further — where the experiment can go next Technical background — optional explanation if you want to know why it works That makes the section useful as both a learning path and an idea library.
snippet: Creative Workflows This is the tips, tricks and experiments section. The normal manual explains what every part of Anvil does. Creative Workflows answers a different ques…

title: Draw Your Own A→B Movement
text: Draw Your Own A→B Movement Draw is useful when the built in curves are close, but the transition needs its own rhythm. Goal Create one IR that moves between A and B in a shape you paint yourself. Build it 1. Load A and B. 2. Click Morph . 3. Enable A→B Lerp . 4. Choose a Morph mode. 5. Set Lerp Start and Lerp Time . 6. Choose Draw . 7. Paint the curve. The bottom of the graph is A. The top is B. The A and B waveforms are visible behind the graph, so you can place the transition around recognizable transients, gaps and tails. Try a return movement Draw something like: The IR can move toward B, return toward A, then move back toward B later. Make the endpoints less obvious Enable F . Now the IR can begin or finish on a blend instead of pure A/pure B. For example: begin around 30% B move to almost pure B return toward A finish around 60% B Refine with nodes Enable N . Add a node with a double click, move it precisely, then use: Shift for fine movement Ctrl for very fine movement Use S when a hand drawn curve needs a smoother transition. Listen for Listen to when the identity changes : does the attack belong to A while the body becomes B? does the middle briefly return to A? does the tail settle into a blend instead of pure B? Push it further Bake the Draw result, load it back into A, then Morph that new IR with something else. That turns one authored movement into raw material for the next generation.

title: Bend Time with Path
text: Bend Time with Path Path can move through the Lerp source time in both directions. One IR can move forward, return to earlier material, then continue forward again. Goal Create an IR with replayed or reversed internal time sections while the A/B blend changes at the same time. Build it 1. Load A and B. 2. Enable A→B Lerp . 3. Choose Path . 4. Set a clear Lerp Start and Lerp Time. 5. Draw from left toward the middle. 6. Move back to the left. 7. Continue toward the right edge. Example: The leftward part reads earlier source time again. Add A/B movement Vertical position still controls A/B blend. So one Path can shape both dimensions: The IR can move toward B while going forward, return toward earlier source time, then continue forward with a different A/B balance. Use the waveforms as landmarks A and B are visible behind the Path editor. Use those waveforms like a map. If you can see a strong event, tail or gap, you can deliberately route the Path through it, return to it, or move toward the other source at exactly that point. This makes Path useful for designed time movement , not only abstract drawing. Use N for precise reversals Enable N . Move an internal node left past another x position. The Path keeps its authored order, so that leftward section remains a backward time route. S keeps the route S smooths the A/B movement without removing the forward/backward time travel. Use it when the vertical blend feels jagged but the timing route is already good. Reset Press R for a straight forward A→B Path. That removes the extra backtracking and returns to normal forward time. Listen for Path can create: repeated internal events reversed fragments inside a forward IR stretched feeling tails without simple time stretching rhythmic returns to an earlier moment A/B changes that happen differently on repeated source time Why the IR can become longer Every backward section adds travel. A straight route reads the Lerp window once. A route that goes forward, backward and forward again reads part of that window more than once, so the rendered IR becomes longer. Push it further Bake a Path IR and use it as one side of a new Morph. A Path generated time structure combined later with Spectral, Stereo Slot Swap or Mid/Side Boundary can create responses whose time and stereo structures were designed in separate generations.

title: Phase & Comb Textures with Color
text: Phase & Comb Textures with Color Color can do much more than create obvious echoes or extra layers. When the Color copy is almost the same length and timing as the original IR , the two versions interfere with each other. Tiny movements can create large tonal changes. This works with almost any IR. Recipe 1 — Time only phase color Goal Create a phasey, metallic or comb like version of an IR without using Offset. Build it 1. Load an IR into A . 2. Click A so you are hearing that slot. 3. Enable C1 . 4. Keep Offset at 0 ms . 5. Move C1 Time slightly away from 1.00 . 6. Try small differences first: around 0.99 / 1.01 , then 0.95 / 1.05 , then further if useful. 7. Adjust Amount by ear. Listen for Do not listen for "more reverb." Listen for the tone itself bending : hollowness, metallic peaks, notches, nasal colors, widening/narrowing impressions, or a completely different cabinet like character. !!! tip The important thing is the difference from 1.00 , not one magic value. A tiny change can be dramatic on one IR and subtle on another. Recipe 2 — Offset only comb color Goal Keep the Color copy at the same length but move it slightly later. Build it 1. Enable C1. 2. Keep Time at 1.00 . 3. Move Offset slowly from about 1–20 ms . 4. Adjust Amount. Listen for Very small offsets can sound like tonal filtering rather than a separate echo. As Offset gets larger, the extra copy starts to feel more like a distinct reflection. Recipe 3 — Mixed Time + Offset phasing Goal Create a less predictable interference pattern by changing both the length and position of the Color copy. Build it 1. Start with C1 Time only slightly different from 1.00 — for example 0.95 or 1.05 . 2. Add a tiny Offset, roughly 1–20 ms . 3. Move Time by very small amounts. 4. Move Offset again. 5. Keep alternating between the two until you hit a useful pocket. Listen for This is where the tone can become very complex because the copy is both drifting in time and starting from a different position . Small movements matter more than large ones. Add C2 Once C1 gives you a useful color: 1. enable C2; 2. keep one Color layer subtle; 3. let the other one use a different Time or Offset relationship. You can create two different interference patterns inside the same IR before Texture or Morph even begins. Add Texture carefully Texture repeats the Color transformation in generations. With a phasey Color setup, even Depth 1 or 2 can become very dense. Do not assume higher Depth is better. Stop when the character becomes useful. Bake the sweet spot If one tiny combination sounds special, Bake it. You can then use that phase colored IR as new source material instead of trying to remember the exact settings. ??? info "Technical background" Color mixes a time resampled and optionally delayed copy of the IR back with the original. When two related signals differ by small amounts in time, some frequencies reinforce while others cancel. The result is frequency dependent comb filtering. Changing Color Time makes that relationship evolve across the IR instead of behaving like a single fixed delay.

title: Found Sounds as IR Material
text: Found Sounds as IR Material A recording does not need to be a measured room response to become useful convolution material. The easiest way to understand this is simply to try it. Good first recordings Record something with a clear character: metal, glass or ceramic hits; cloth, paper or leaves; doors, tools and mechanical objects; water, gravel or footsteps; a clap or snap in an unusual room; a breath or short vocal sound; a short noise or texture. Build it 1. Load the recording into A . 2. Click A so you are hearing it. 3. Use Start/End to isolate one interesting region. 4. Link Start and End if you want to scan a fixed size window through the recording. 5. Fade the edges if the cut feels too abrupt. 6. Try Color or Texture. 7. Use EQ only if the material needs cleanup. 8. Bake several promising versions. Listen for the small moments A long recording may sound obviously like "a recording." A tiny part of the same file can behave like something completely different: a resonant filter; a strange cabinet; a sharp transient space; a metallic tonal fingerprint; a tiny impossible room. That is why EDIT is so useful with found sounds. Scan instead of guessing Create a short Start/End window and link it. Then move the window through the recording while audio plays. Shift + drag = fine Ctrl + drag = very fine When a position suddenly does something interesting to the track, stop and Bake it. Push it further Take one good fragment and: phase color it with ; Morph it with a normal room IR; Bake it and use it again; create several different fragments from the same recording and Morph those together.

title: Recursive Baking
text: Recursive Baking A Bake does not have to be the final result. It can become the next ingredient . The basic idea Make something: Then load C back into Anvil: Then do it again: By G, the original ingredients may no longer be obvious at all. Build it 1. Create a useful A/B result. 2. Bake it. 3. Load that Bake back into A. 4. Put a different source in B. 5. Change the Morph mode, Color, EDIT region or stereo treatment. 6. Bake again. Do not make only one lineage Instead of: try branches: Branches give you more different material to recombine later. Keep generations under control Recursive design can quickly become dense. When that happens: use EDIT to keep only the useful section; Normalize deliberately; use HP/LP to remove useless buildup; compare against an earlier generation; stop adding layers when the new Bake is only "more" rather than better. Strong combination Recursive Baking becomes especially powerful with , because each generation can preserve a different spatial relationship before the next Morph begins.

title: Multi-Morph Stereo Worlds
text: Multi Morph Stereo Worlds One Morph does not have to be the end of the design. Because Anvil can Bake the result, you can create one stereo relationship, freeze it into a new IR, then combine that new IR with another differently built response. This is multi morphing . Basic multi morph Goal Build a response whose stereo and tonal behavior comes from more than one Morph generation. Build it 1. Load A and B. 2. Choose Stereo Slot Swap . 3. Move Morph toward a useful A left / B right relationship rather than automatically centering it. 4. Bake that result as IR 1 . 5. Create another result from two sources—new ones or the same ones. 6. Use a different Morph mode. 7. Bake it as IR 2 . 8. Load IR 1 into A and IR 2 into B. 9. Morph those two Bakes again—for example with Spectral . 10. Bake the new generation. What happened? The last Morph is no longer working with two simple source IRs. It is working with two already designed soundfields . That is why the result can become much more complex than one Morph pass. Advanced recipe — Stereo Slot Swap + Mid/Side Boundary + Spectral This is a strong starting recipe for very large or unusual stereo responses. Stage 1 — build a left/right relationship 1. Load two interesting IRs. 2. Choose Stereo Slot Swap . 3. Find a position where the A/B relationship gives you useful left/right contrast. 4. Bake it as StereoSwap.wav . Stereo Slot Swap lets the left side travel A→B while the right side travels B→A, so the two sides can carry different source relationships. Stage 2 — build a center/side relationship 1. Load two other sources—or reuse the same ones with different settings. 2. Choose Mid/Side Boundary . 3. Find a position where A gives you a strong center and B gives you an interesting outside field. 4. Bake it as MidSide.wav . Stage 3 — morph the two finished soundfields 1. Load StereoSwap.wav into A. 2. Load MidSide.wav into B. 3. Start with Time Morph just to hear the two complete structures together. 4. Then try Spectral . 5. Move Morph slowly. 6. Bake anything that creates a stereo world you could not get from either generation alone. Why this can become huge You are combining: a response where left and right already carry different A/B relationships; a response with a deliberate center/side structure; then a third Morph operation that combines those finished responses again. The result can contain a dense center, different side information, and spectral changes across a stereo field that was already complex before the final Morph began. !!! tip "Do not chase maximum width" Huge does not always mean useful. Check the result in context with your track and pull Width back if the center starts feeling weak or disconnected. Push it further After the final Bake: put the result back into A and add a room IR in B; use Color with tiny Time differences on only one generation; use EDIT to keep only the best section of the final stereo response; reverse a fragment; create two branches and Morph those branches again. That is the point where an IR can become a designed sound world rather than a recognizable mixture of its original sources. ??? info "Technical background" Stereo Slot Swap processes the left field from A toward B while the right field travels from B toward A. Mid/Side Boundary keeps A as the center foundation while B contributes the side field. Baking each stage collapses that processing into new stereo IR data, so a later Morph treats the already complex outputs as new source material.

title: Create a Theme from an Image with AI
text: Create a Theme from an Image with AI You can create a complete Impulse Anvil theme without manually choosing every color. Use any image whose mood, contrast and color balance you like as a visual reference, then let an AI translate that look into an Impulse Anvil Theme Schema 2 file. Goal Turn a visual reference into a usable Impulse Anvil theme. Examples: a game screenshot album artwork a photograph a UI you like a color palette your own artwork a screenshot of a room, landscape or object with a strong mood The image does not become part of Impulse Anvil. It is only used as a design reference for the theme colors. What you need 1. Impulse Anvil 2. an exported Theme Schema 2 JSON file 3. one reference image 4. an AI that can read both the JSON and the image Build it 1. Export a Theme Schema 2 file In Impulse Anvil open: Options → Design → Export Current Theme Save the JSON somewhere easy to find. This gives the AI the exact structure Impulse Anvil expects. 2. Give the AI the JSON and your reference image Upload both files together. Then use a prompt like: Generate an Impulse Anvil Theme Schema 2 that matches the mood, contrast and color relationships of this image. Keep the JSON structure and all required keys exactly compatible with Impulse Anvil. Return only the finished JSON. 3. Replace the JSON content Open the exported theme file in a text editor. Replace its contents with the JSON generated by the AI and save the file. Then import it in Impulse Anvil: Options → Design → Import Theme JSON Your new design is ready to try. Make the result more specific Once the first theme works, you can ask for variations. For example: Make the Morph section more prominent while keeping A and B quieter. Keep the same mood but increase readability. Make the highlights less saturated. Give A and B different accents while keeping the whole theme coherent. Make it darker and more minimal. Keep the palette but increase contrast around active controls. Because Theme Schema 2 supports separate colors for A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT, the AI can create more than a single global palette. Generate themes without a reference image You can also upload only the Theme Schema 2 JSON and ask: Generate three high quality Impulse Anvil themes with clearly different moods. Keep the schema fully compatible. Then try them in Anvil and keep the one that fits your music or workspace best. Design for the mood you want to work in The visual design does not change the audio, but it changes how the workspace feels. A dark, restrained theme can feel very different from a bright high contrast theme. A cold metallic design can suit a different session than a warm, muted one. Theme design is therefore not only decoration. It is a way to make Impulse Anvil feel like your own instrument and workspace . !!! tip "Use references, not copies" The strongest results usually come from asking the AI to translate the mood, palette, contrast and hierarchy of an image rather than reproduce someone else's design literally. Keep a small theme library When a generated theme works well: 1. save the JSON; 2. give it a clear name; 3. keep a few different moods available; 4. switch themes when the project or session changes. Over time you can build your own Impulse Anvil design library without needing to design every theme by hand.

title: FAQ
text: FAQ Can I use ordinary recordings as impulse responses? Yes. Impulse Anvil can load compatible audio material and use it as convolution material. Short intentional fragments are usually easier to control than long unedited recordings. Can I take a tiny part from the tail of an IR and export it? Yes. Use Start and End to isolate the region. Link them when you want to scan a fixed length window through a longer response, then press Bake . Can I reverse only one selected region? Yes. Move Start later than End . The region between the endpoints becomes a reversed slice. Can I morph two IRs and save the result? Yes. Load A and B, click Morph , choose the relationship you want, then press Bake . Can an IR evolve from A to B inside one file? Yes. Enable A→B Lerp . The selected Morph mode and curve define how the response develops from A toward B over time. Are Lerp Start and Lerp Time percentages? No. They are absolute milliseconds . Lerp Start = when the transition begins Lerp Time = how long it takes Lerp Time can be 0 ms for an instant switch. Can I draw my own Morph/Lerp curve? Yes. Choose Draw in the Curve menu and paint the A/B movement directly. Use U/S/N/F/R for Undo, Smooth, precision Nodes, Free endpoints and Reset. Can Draw start or end on a blend instead of pure A/B? Yes. Enable F in Draw. The first and last points can then sit anywhere between A and B. What does Path do? Path controls both A/B blend and source time travel . Moving right reads later source time. Moving left reads earlier source time again, so a Path can create replayed or reversed sections inside the new IR. Why can Path make the IR longer? A straight Path reads the Lerp time span once. Horizontal backtracking adds extra travel through that span, so the rendered IR becomes longer. Does Path work in Bake? Yes. Path Preview and Bake use the same prepared Path result. What are the waveforms behind the Draw/Path graph? They show the current A and B source shapes behind the curve editor. Use them as visual landmarks when drawing transitions or Path routes—for example, to line up a blend change with a transient, return to an earlier event, or follow a tail by eye. Can I load a baked IR back into Anvil? Yes. A Bake is a standard WAV file, so it can become A or B in another design pass. Is there a separate Bake A→B button? No. The current interface uses one Bake button for every prepared state, including Lerp, Draw and Path. Does Out change the exported WAV? No. Out is final playback output only. IR In changes the prepared/baked IR level. Does Dry/Wet change the exported WAV? No. Dry/Wet and Wet Level affect how you hear the plugin on the track, not the IR stored by Bake. Does 0 ms Fade still change the endpoint? No. Fade In = 0 ms or Fade Out = 0 ms leaves that endpoint unshaped. How far can Color Offset go? Color Offset runs from 0–500 ms . Tiny offsets are useful for phase/comb tone. Larger values can create clearly separated secondary events. Does Anvil remember where I browse for IRs? Yes. A successful manual load remembers that folder and uses it as the first choice next time. Can I customize A, B and the other panels separately? Yes. Open Options → Design → Customize Current Theme… and enable panel specific colors for A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT or OUT. Can I export a theme? Yes. Use Options → Design → Export Current Theme . The exported JSON can be edited, shared and imported again. How do I switch between hearing A, B and Morph? Click the A , B or Morph panel. Can I make tiny millisecond adjustments more easily? Yes. Hold Shift before dragging for fine movement or Ctrl before dragging for very fine movement. What can Align remove? Align can shift a source so its important peak begins earlier. If useful material existed before that peak, that pre peak material can be lost. Compare Align on and off when the lead in matters. How do I reset only one part of Anvil? Double click Color , EQ , EDIT or OUT to reset that section. To reset the whole control state while keeping A/B files loaded, use Options → Init / Reset Controls (keep IRs) .

title: Troubleshooting
text: Troubleshooting Bake says “Nothing to export” A prepared IR is not ready yet. Load A, or load A+B and enable Morph/A→B Lerp. If you just made a heavy change, let the preview finish rebuilding and press Bake again. A change takes longer on a long IR Controls that rebuild the impulse response may need to process many samples, spectral transforms and recursive Color/Texture layers. Trim the useful region earlier when possible. My Bake level does not follow Out That is expected. Out is playback only . Use IR In , slot gains or IR Normalize when you want to change the exported response level. Texture does nothing Texture needs an enabled Color transformation. Set Texture Depth above 0 and enable C1 or C2 in that same slot. A→B Lerp disabled the Morph knob That is intentional. Lerp is not a single global A/B position; it changes state across the IR's own time axis. Curve, K and Lerp Time define that progression. My external source does not restore in an old project Impulse Anvil stores file paths for externally loaded IRs. Keep the files available at the same location or reload them manually.

title: Technical Background
text: Technical Background This section collects implementation details that are useful for deeper reference. The normal feature pages remain producer facing. Slot preparation order 1. time stretch 2. Color / Texture construction 3. optional per slot Normalize 4. slot Gain Gain therefore remains meaningful while a slot's Normalize switch is enabled. Color Color resamples the source to create a time scaled copy, applies a sample offset and gain, then sums that copy back with the source. Color Offset now has a 0–500 ms user range. Texture Texture is recursive Color. Each generated layer becomes input to the next generation. Depth is 0–4. Time Morph and Align Time Morph interpolates sample values between A and B. Align can left shift participating time domain material toward sample zero. Material that originally occurred before the moved peak can therefore be lost. Spectral Morph Spectral modes transform the sources into frequency domain representations, combine spectral information, and reconstruct a causal response. Absolute Lerp timing 1.0.121 uses Lerp Start and Lerp Time in milliseconds. The visible UI domain follows the current prepared A/B endpoint duration, including Time and Color/Texture length growth. Start reduces the remaining available Time range. Draw Draw stores a normalized A/B curve. With Free off, the first point is A=0 and the last point is B=1. With Free on, the first/last y values may sit anywhere from 0–1. Outside the active Lerp timing window, the authored free endpoint value is held. Path Path stores an ordered list of normalized (x, y) points: x = source time position inside the Lerp window y = A/B blend point order = output traversal order The renderer accumulates absolute horizontal travel. Leftward x movement is preserved, so earlier source time is read again rather than being sorted away. A straight 0→1 path uses the normal span. Backtracking adds output frames. Exact endpoints Hidden authored head/tail micro fades were removed from the Color/preview/prepared paths. A user Fade value of 0 ms leaves that endpoint unshaped. Runtime convolver switching remains click protected separately. Post/Sculpt order slice/reverse → fades → predelay → IR In → HP/LP/Bells/Tilt → Width → Normalize → IR side limiter Final Dry/Wet mixing, Wet Level and final Out happen later and are not part of Bake. Theme Schema 2 Global colors remain the base theme. A, B, Morph, EQ, EDIT and OUT may each optionally override panel, panelStroke, accent, highlight, knob and text colors. Disabled panel overrides inherit Global values.
